slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code creates and appends a stylesheet link element to the document head, fetches the '../template.html' file via the fetch API, reads its content as text, and uses it to instantiate a test fixture, facilitating automated accessibility testing of a web component.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code dynamically appends a local stylesheet link and fetches a local HTML template to instantiate a test fixture for automated accessibility testing. Unlike the known malicious patterns, it does not load resources from external or attacker-controlled domains, nor does it execute or download binaries, perform redirects, or engage in obfuscated or hidden malicious activities. The use of fetch and DOM manipulation here is legitimate and typical for testing environments. The closest similarity (Example 1) involves loading external stylesheets from untrusted domains, which is not the case here since the stylesheet and template are loaded from relative local paths. There is no evidence of suspicious behavior such as data exfiltration, system manipulation, or hidden payload execution.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (template rendering), the code loads a stylesheet from an external domain (fonts.googleapis.com), causing the application to make a network request to fetch remote CSS, which could be replaced with malicious content.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading CSS from an external, uncontrolled domain introduces the risk that the remote resource could be modified to deliver malicious payloads, such as CSS-based exfiltration or further script injection if the server is compromised.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard application templates should only reference trusted, vetted, or self-hosted assets. Loading resources from external domains not under organizational control increases the risk of supply chain attacks and content injection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use includes loading fonts or stylesheets from well-known, trusted CDNs (e.g., Google Fonts), but only when the CDN is explicitly trusted and the risk is assessed.
key_indicators: External stylesheet loaded at runtime
Reference to fonts.googleapis.com in HTML <link> tag
Network request to a domain not under organizational control
Potential for remote content replacement or injection

attack_chain.action: Application template loads an external stylesheet from fonts.googleapis.com at runtime.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for an attacker to replace or inject malicious CSS or further payloads via the external resource, increasing the risk of content injection or data exfiltration.

behavioral_signatures: Loading external stylesheets or scripts from remote domains in application templates
Presence of <link> or <script> tags referencing non-whitelisted domains in HTML files
file_indicators: templates/*.html files containing <link> tags with href attributes pointing to external domains (e.g., fonts.googleapis.com)
Configuration or template files referencing domains not on an approved whitelist
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to fonts.googleapis.com or other non-whitelisted domains during template rendering
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan HTML template files for <link> or <script> tags referencing external domains not on an approved whitelist. Monitor runtime network activity for outbound requests to non-whitelisted domains such as fonts.googleapis.com. Flag any executable or style content loaded from remote sources that are not explicitly approved by security policy.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the browser loads and executes JavaScript from cdn.polyfill.io, which initiates network requests to attacker-controlled or typosquatted domains, resulting in user redirection or additional malicious payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The CDN, previously trusted, now serves scripts that perform unauthorized actions such as redirecting users and loading code from lookalike domains, which is a significant deviation from its original purpose.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A CDN-hosted polyfill script should only provide browser compatibility code and must not perform redirects, inject additional scripts, or communicate with suspicious domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate CDNs serve static polyfill or analytics scripts without redirecting users or referencing non-official domains.
key_indicators: Script loaded from cdn.polyfill.io performs unexpected redirects
References to typosquatted or attacker-controlled domains in loaded scripts
Behavioral change after domain ownership transfer

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when <script src="cdn.polyfill.io"> is loaded by the browser)
execution_context.file_location: Injected via remote script from cdn.polyfill.io, included in the HTML of victim websites

package_info.package_versions: all versions after February 2024 (post-acquisition by Funnull)
package_info.why_malicious: After the domain cdn.polyfill.io was acquired by Funnull in February 2024, the CDN began serving modified JavaScript that injects malicious code into any website embedding it. This code redirects users to spam or malicious sites, loads additional payloads from attacker-controlled or typosquatted domains, and leverages anti-analysis techniques to evade detection. The attack abuses the trust in a previously reputable CDN to compromise a large number of websites.

attack_chain.action: Website includes <script src="cdn.polyfill.io">, loading remote JavaScript.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious script is executed in the user's browser.

attack_chain.action: Malicious script from cdn.polyfill.io fetches and executes additional code from typosquatted domains (e.g., googie-analytics.com).
attack_chain.leads_to: User may be redirected or further payloads may be executed.

attack_chain.action: Malicious script checks if the user is an admin and avoids execution if detected, to evade analysis.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious actions are only performed on non-admin users, reducing detection risk.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected redirects or script loads from websites using cdn.polyfill.io
Loading of JavaScript from typosquatted domains such as googie-analytics.com
Conditional execution logic in scripts to evade admin or analysis environments
file_indicators: References to googie-analytics.com or other lookalike domains in loaded scripts
network_indicators: Requests to other suspicious or typosquatted domains (e.g., kuurza.com)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan website source code and network traffic for inclusion of cdn.polyfill.io and references to typosquatted domains. Monitor for unexpected redirects or script loads, especially from domains that closely resemble legitimate services (e.g., Google Analytics). Use web application firewalls or browser security tools to block or alert on requests to known malicious or typosquatted domains. Implement automated scanning for conditional execution logic that attempts to evade admin or analysis environments.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code loads legitimate speed test modules to provide expected functionality, while simultaneously downloading and executing a mining binary in the background, which connects to a mining pool and hijacks system resources for mining.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code blends legitimate speed test functionality with hidden malicious mining activity, a classic trojanization technique. The malicious process is launched in the background to avoid user detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A speed test utility should not execute unrelated binaries or initiate background mining processes while providing legitimate functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for this behavior exists in a speed test utility. Blending benign and malicious code is a hallmark of trojanized packages.
key_indicators: Blending of legitimate and malicious code in the same file
Background mining process launched alongside expected functionality
External binary download and execution
Outbound connection to mining pool

package_info.package_versions: all versions published by user 'trendava' before Jan 18, 2023
package_info.why_malicious: These packages impersonate legitimate internet speed testing utilities but instead deploy cryptocurrency miners, covertly hijacking system resources for unauthorized mining operations. The packages employ multiple evasion techniques, including downloading mining binaries from external sources, embedding miners, dynamically retrieving mining pool addresses, and blending malicious activity with legitimate functionality to avoid detection.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious NPM package, believing it to be a legitimate speed test utility.
Malicious code in index.js executes at import-time, downloading a mining binary from an external source (such as GitLab or an external IP).
attack_chain.leads_to: Binary is made executable and launched

attack_chain.action: The mining binary is executed, connecting to a cryptocurrency mining pool (address may be hardcoded or dynamically retrieved from an external source).
attack_chain.leads_to: System resources are hijacked for mining

attack_chain.action: In some variants, legitimate speed test functionality is provided to avoid suspicion and maintain user trust.
attack_chain.leads_to: User is unaware of background mining activity

behavioral_signatures: NPM package executes code at import-time or install-time, triggering process execution without user interaction
Downloads and executes external binaries from untrusted sources such as GitLab or direct IP addresses
Initiates outbound connections to known mining pool addresses or suspicious IPs, including WebSocket connections
Blends legitimate speed test functionality with hidden mining activity in the same codebase
file_indicators: index.js containing exec, wget, curl, chmod, or nohup commands
Presence of downloaded binaries named 'data', 'los', or 'miner' in the package directory
Unexpected use of process execution functions (e.g., exec) in JavaScript files of speed test utilities
network_indicators: Outbound connections to mining pool addresses such as eu.kaspa.k1pool.com:15555 and 51.222.96.66:80
Dynamic retrieval of mining pool addresses from external IPs via HTTP or curl
WebSocket connections to suspicious IPs for mining activity
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor NPM package installations and imports for scripts that download and execute external binaries, especially from non-standard or untrusted sources. Flag packages that initiate outbound connections to known mining pools or suspicious IPs, or use exec/spawn to run shell commands. Inspect for blended code that provides expected speed test functionality while launching background processes. Use static and dynamic analysis to detect unexpected process creation, file downloads, and network activity during package installation or import. Correlate presence of binaries named 'data', 'los', or 'miner' with suspicious process and network behavior.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.
key_indicators: Presence of ---js front matter blocks in Markdown input
Arbitrary JavaScript execution during Markdown parsing
Direct filesystem access via require('fs').readFileSync in user-supplied content
Injection of sensitive file contents into user-facing output (PDF)
Lack of input sanitization or code execution restrictions in Markdown processing

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits specially crafted Markdown containing a ---js front matter block with malicious JavaScript to the invoice generator.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

attack_chain.action: The malicious JavaScript reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (flag) is loaded into memory during document generation.

attack_chain.action: The code injects the flag value into the CSS of the generated PDF document.
attack_chain.leads_to: Flag is exfiltrated to the attacker via the exported PDF file.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of arbitrary JavaScript during Markdown-to-PDF conversion
Access to sensitive files (e.g., /flag.txt) from within Markdown processing
User-controlled input leading to server-side code execution during document generation
file_indicators: Markdown files or input containing ---js front matter blocks
References to require('fs') or other Node.js modules in user-supplied Markdown content
network_indicators: Unusual outbound connections initiated during Markdown processing (if exfiltration is attempted via network)
No direct network indicators in this specific exploit, but possible in variants where exfiltration is performed over the network
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of ---js front matter in Markdown inputs, especially when processed by md-to-pdf or gray-matter. Audit application logs for unexpected file access (e.g., /flag.txt) during document generation. Use static analysis to detect unsafe use of gray-matter with JS engine enabled. Block or sanitize user-supplied front matter in Markdown, and upgrade md-to-pdf to a version that disables arbitrary code execution. Implement strict input validation and disable JavaScript execution in Markdown processing libraries.

matched_knowledge.source_package: standforusz, react-vuejs, tetusdgsudgs, jqueryoffline, vueofflinez, jquerydownloadnew (npm)

matched_snippet.code_snippet:
<script src="jquery.js"></script>
// jquery.js fetches jquery.min.js from CDN, which then fetches DEMO.txt and writes its content (fake login form) to the document.
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads jquery.js, which fetches additional JavaScript and text files from a remote CDN, reads DEMO.txt containing a fake Microsoft login form, injects the form into the DOM, and enables credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and dynamically injecting remote content to display a credential harvesting form is a well-known phishing technique, especially when the content mimics Microsoft login pages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject fake login forms or exfiltrate user credentials, nor should they fetch and execute remote scripts without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic content loading is common for legitimate widgets or analytics, but not for credential forms or authentication interfaces.
key_indicators: Dynamic fetching of remote scripts and text files
Injection of fake Microsoft login forms into the DOM
Credential exfiltration logic targeting attacker infrastructure
Use of misleading file names (e.g., jquery.js) to mimic legitimate libraries

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a malicious HTML attachment is opened in the browser)
execution_context.file_location: jquery.js (from standforusz package, used in phishing email attachments)

package_info.package_name: standforusz, react-vuejs, tetusdgsudgs, jqueryoffline, vueofflinez, jquerydownloadnew
package_info.package_versions: standforusz: 1.0.2, 1.0.3, 1.0.4, 3.0.7, 3.0.10; react-vuejs: 3.0.10, 10.21.30; tetusdgsudgs: 1.0.3, 1.0.4, 1.0.5; jqueryoffline: 1.0.2; vueofflinez: 1.0.1; jquerydownloadnew: 1.0.1
package_info.why_malicious: These npm packages were intentionally crafted to either serve as phishing kit infrastructure or implant credential harvesting scripts into applications. They target end users by mimicking legitimate libraries, using obfuscated code to inject fake Microsoft login forms, and exfiltrating credentials to attacker-controlled infrastructure. The packages are distributed via npm and are designed to be included in phishing email attachments or as supply chain implants in web applications.

attack_chain.action: Malicious npm package is published and distributed, either as phishing kit infrastructure or as a supply chain implant in developer applications.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious files are included in phishing emails or embedded in web applications.

attack_chain.action: Victim opens a malicious HTML attachment or uses an application containing the malicious package, triggering execution of the embedded JavaScript.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JavaScript is executed in the victim's browser or application environment.

attack_chain.action: Malicious JavaScript fetches and injects a fake Microsoft login form into the DOM, often overlaying a blurred document to prompt for credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is presented with a convincing fake login prompt.

attack_chain.action: Victim enters credentials into the fake form, which are then collected and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials are sent to external domains or IPs controlled by the attacker.

attack_chain.action: Anti-analysis code disables right-click and developer tools to hinder user inspection and detection of the phishing activity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Reduces likelihood of user or analyst discovering the phishing activity or analyzing the malicious code.

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated JavaScript in npm package entry points (e.g., use of eval and encoded variable names)
Dynamic fetching and injection of remote HTML/JS content at runtime
Creation and injection of fake login forms mimicking Microsoft 365 or other authentication portals
Credential exfiltration via HTTP POST to non-corporate domains or hardcoded IP addresses
Disabling of browser right-click context menu and developer tools through JavaScript event handlers
file_indicators: Presence of DEMO.txt, index.html, or index.js files in npm packages
Obfuscated or hex-encoded JavaScript in main entry files (e.g., index.js)
Form actions or JavaScript POST requests pointing to ourwhite.brainleeches.xyz or 137.184.153.238
Files named to mimic legitimate libraries (e.g., jquery.js) but containing malicious logic
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests containing credential data to non-corporate endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that contain obfuscated JavaScript, especially in main entry points or files named after popular libraries (e.g., jquery.js). Flag packages containing DEMO.txt, index.html, or index.js files with embedded credential forms. Detect network traffic to known malicious domains or IPs (ourwhite.brainleeches.xyz, 137.184.153.238) and monitor for HTTP POST requests with credential data to these endpoints. Use static and dynamic analysis to identify code that disables browser inspection tools or dynamically injects login forms. Correlate file, behavioral, and network indicators to identify and block malicious packages before they are executed.
